 Live Updates: Midterm voters go to the polls on Election Day
 Politics 
 Updated on Nov 3, 2026 5:36 PM EST — Published on
 Nov 3, 2026 11:00 AM EST
 2026 ELECTION COVERAGE: Watch Live | Poll Closing Times | All Live Results | Live Updates | Live Fact Check 
 Election Day is here. Voters nationwide will decide control of the U.S. House and Senate. Democrats must flip four seats in the Senate and three seats in the House to wrest control of the chambers from Republicans. Control of Congress would give Democrats a way to push back against President Donald Trump's agenda during the final two years of his term. The battle for control is playing out mostly in states and districts Trump previously won by wide margins.
 WATCH LIVE: Election night 2026 PBS News special coverage 
 All eyes are on Senate contests in Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Ohio and Texas, while House battlegrounds are scattered across the country.
 Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News 
 Democrats have homed in on Trump's poor approval rating, public dissatisfaction with the war in Iran and affordability concerns. Republicans have focused on social issues, while Trump has made himself the central character of the midterms.
 Here's the latest.
 5:36 p.m. EST
 House races to watch: Districts that flipped in 2024
 The handful of House members who flipped the toughest seats in 2024 all face challenging races again this year. Can they avoid a sophomore slump?
 WATCH: Mapping the battle for control of the House 
 Most of these districts flipped to the GOP in 2024, riding Trump's coattails as he clinched a second term. The good news for these Republicans is that it's almost always easier to win a seat that you already represent. The bad news is that many of them won their seats by tiny margins and are facing a much tougher national environment this time around.
 DOJ escalates criminal investigation of Alaska Senate candidate
 The Trump administration notified prominent Democratic attorney Marc Elias and others that they may be targets of the inquiry, which focuses on a Senate candidate who shares a name with the Republican incumbent.
 That's according to two people familiar with the matter, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss an ongoing investigation.
 READ MORE: FBI visits Dan J. Sullivan donor in candidate's hometown as Alaska Senate inquiry widens 
 Trump's DOJ is investigating retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan's decision to run for Senate, which the president says will confuse voters because he shares a first and last name with Republican incumbent Dan S. Sullivan. The New York Times reported that Democrat Mary Peltola's campaign appeared to be involved in recruiting Dan J. Sullivan.
 "This administration has repeatedly weaponized the DOJ against the President's political enemies despite zero evidence of wrongdoing, and we are the latest targets," Elias said in a statement Tuesday.
 Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, Republican candidate for reelection, accompanied by his wife Julie Fate Sullivan, arrives to vote during the midterm elections, in Anchorage, Alaska, Nov. 3, 2026. Photo by Emily Mesner/Reuters
 4:41 p.m. EST
 Immigration enforcement agency issues warning to voters
 Federal immigration officials took to social media on Election Day to warn against illegal voting by noncitizens.
 In a message on X, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement wrote: "If you vote illegally, we will find you. We will track you down, arrest you, and prosecute you. There will be no escape."
 The agency did not return messages seeking comment about the post. Throughout Tuesday, it also posted about arrests of noncitizens accused of voting.
 While that has been a major emphasis for the agency this year, the number of arrests and earlier investigations in the states demonstrate the problem is rare.
 READ MORE: Justice Department urges sanctions for database analysis critical of its noncitizen voting claims 
 David Becker, executive director of the Center for Election Innovation & Research, called the post unfortunate but said heavy early voting suggested the administration's tactics appeared to have no effect on turnout.
 "If there were individuals in this administration who thought that they could scare voters away from this election, they're going to be disappointed," he said.
 Incumbents in redrawn districts face very different electorates than in 2024
 Many incumbents running for reelection in redrawn districts are facing a very different set of voters than they currently represent.
 Several districts went from being majority-nonwhite to majority-white after mid-decade redistricting. These are also some of the places that shifted the most toward Trump when comparing the 2024 vote margin under old and new congressional boundaries.
 Similarly, a number of districts shifted from being majority-white to being majority-nonwhite. Many of these districts also shifted toward Harris, but some in Texas and Florida moved further to the right.
 4:16 p.m. EST
 Michigan raised concerns about federal monitors in two cities
 Michigan election officials objected after hearing that federal poll monitors in Dearborn and Flint were asking workers about their training or requesting to see training materials, a spokesperson said.
 "This is not permitted under the law," said Angela Benander of the Department of State.
 The U.S. Justice Department agreed and pledged to inform the election monitors, Benander said.
 Separately, she said federal monitors in Lansing were trying to talk to voters, which is OK if the exchange happens after a ballot is cast and is outside the polling place.
 "We don't have any concerns," Benander said.
 4:11 p.m. EST
 3 precincts in Pennsylvania extend voting hours due to machine issues
 Officials in Pennsylvania's Chester County say they're extending voting hours in three precincts after "machine set-up issues" delayed the opening of polling sites just west of Philadelphia.
 The Chester County Court of Common Pleas granted the three precincts a 30-minute extension, meaning voters will be able to cast ballots until 8:30 p.m. EST, according to the county.
 Voters casting ballots at these three sites after 8 p.m. EST — when polling stations close statewide — will use provisional ballots.
 5 polling sites will stay open late in North Carolina
 Election officials extended voting hours at each location after county election supervisors reported delays caused by technical problems with computers.
 The longest extension granted by the North Carolina State Board of Elections was 45 minutes at one location in Columbus County, where officials said computer problems forced election workers to switch to backup paper poll books, slowing lines Tuesday morning.
 Two precincts in Hertford County and one each in Lenoir and Wilson counties also will stay open an extra 15 to 30 minutes. The five-member board approved each extension unanimously.
 The extended hours mean state election officials in North Carolina won't begin reporting results until after the last polling site closes at 8:15 p.m. ET, said Adam Steele, an attorney for the election board. He said county election officials will tally their votes without delay.
 Polls in North Carolina close at 7:30 p.m. ET, unless extended by the board.
 Latest views on the 2 major parties from AP-NORC polling
 At least half of U.S. adults have a negative opinion of the two parties, according to AP-NORC polling.
 About half have a "very" or "somewhat" unfavorable view of the Democratic Party in an AP-NORC poll from October, while just over half say that about the Republican Party.
 Roughly 7 in 10 Democrats hold a favorable view of their own party, which is down from 85% in September 2024. Republicans, however, feel about as positively as they did two years ago, with 85% in the latest polling saying they have a favorable view of the Republican Party.
 Only about 2 in 10 U.S. adults feel "very" or "somewhat" optimistic about the future of the Democratic Party or the Republican Party. Republicans are a bit more optimistic about their party's future than Democrats are — slightly fewer than half of Republicans, 46%, say they are feeling positive, compared to 35% of Democrats.
 3:58 p.m. EST
 In Texas, Korean vet voter weighs in on Iran war
 In southeastern Texas, Juventino Sáenz accompanied a relative to the polls in McAllen.
 The 91-year-old Korean War veteran who said he'd voted early shared his feelings about Trump's decision to go to war with Iran.
 Sáenz blamed Iran but also blamed Trump, saying the president should have gone to Congress for permission.
 "He couldn't do it just because he's the president," Sáenz said.
 He said he's backed Republicans in the past, citing his votes for Ronald Reagan and George H.W. Bush for president.
 But in the closely watched Texas U.S. Senate race, Sáenz said he voted for Talarico, the Democrat, because he didn't like Paxton's record or that Paxton's own Republican Party impeached him.
 "He was doing a lot of things that were not right," he said of Paxton.
 Pain at the pump powers voter fury
 Gas prices have shot up by nearly a third since Trump launched his war against Iran, fueling voter distress about the economy and high prices. But another fuel source has risen even higher and caused potentially more pain.
 That's diesel fuel, which powers not just a whole bunch of farming and industrial equipment but the ships and trucks that transport a range of goods and services to voters' doors.
 READ MORE: Trump administration promised farmers $15 billion in weeks before midterms 
 Diesel prices have nearly doubled since the start of the Iran war. A disproportionate share of the oil that comes through the Strait of Hormuz is used to make diesel. Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries that produce the fuel added to the shortage.
 That pushed Trump to take controversial action to try to lower the price of diesel, cutting a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to sell diesel from his country to the U.S. But even that hasn't significantly brought diesel prices down.
 3:38 p.m. EST
 Ranks of Black governors could grow with 8 nominees nationwide
 Maryland's Wes Moore is the only Black governor in the U.S., and he's only the third elected Black governor in history, all of them Democrats and men.
 But Moore, who's heavily favored for reelection, could soon have company.
 There are seven additional Black major party nominees for governor. They include Republicans and Democrats, men and women. Each would be the first Black chief executive in their respective states.
 Georgia's Keisha Lance Bottoms, the former Atlanta mayor and a Democrat, and Minnesota's Lisa Demuth, a former state legislative leader and a Republican, could each make history. No Black woman has ever been elected as governor.
 LIVE RESULTS: Georgia governor midterm election 
 Two Black Republican men are on gubernatorial ballots: Byron Donalds in Florida and John James in Michigan. Both are U.S. representatives currently.
 Three other Black men, all Democrats, round out the slate: Aaron Ford in Nevada, Jermaine Johnson in South Carolina and David Crowley in Wisconsin.
 Early vote count reaches nearly 60 million as Election Day voting continues
 More than 59 million people have voted so far, according to an Associated Press analysis.
 The advance vote has spiked ahead of Election Day compared to 2022. There were 59.7 million ballots cast as of Tuesday, compared to a little over 58 million in 2022.
 The tally includes early in-person and mail balloting.
 The election will determine which party controls the House and Senate.
 A Trump-backed redistricting plan goes to voters
 At Trump's urging, Republicans in eight states adopted new congressional districts to try to gain an edge in the midterm elections. But after a long legal battle, Missouri's new map was blocked by both the U.S. Supreme Court and the Missouri Supreme Court because of a referendum petition.
 Voters are now deciding whether to uphold or reject the new map. If approved, it could be used in the 2028 election.
 Maryland voters are deciding a constitutional amendment that also could pave the way for a new House map in the 2028 election. Democratic proponents have urged a "yes" vote as a means to "stop Trump."
 READ MORE: About 35 million people have been put into new House districts in the fight over congressional maps, report says 
 Some Colorado Democrats also want to redistrict. But a citizen initiative on the ballot there would prohibit any potential redistricting for 2028 from favoring one political party and require approval from both an independent commission and the state Supreme Court.
 Some voters in Georgia receive false texts from an unknown sender about polling site changes
 A few hiccups have come up in Fulton County, Georgia, a Democratic stronghold Trump has long falsely accused of widespread voter fraud that he says caused him to lose the state in 2020.
 Some voters have reported receiving texts that were not sent by the county about polling place changes, according to Fulton County's Facebook page. A county spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for more information.
 Kyle Gomez-Leineweber, policy director at election watchdog group Common Cause Georgia, said the group was aware of the texts but didn't know who sent them or if they were based on incorrect information or were intentionally trying to mislead voters.
 Gomez-Leineweber said volunteers have been telling people to double-check information with official sources.
 Separately, about 1,000 ballots received during early voting last month will be rescanned "as a precaution" due to equipment failures with two scanners, Georgia Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger said Tuesday. He said it would not delay election results.
 Progressive Democrats try flipping swing House districts
 Election workers extract mail-in ballots for the midterm election at the Registrar of Voters in San Diego, California, on Nov. 3, 2026. Photo by Mike Blake/ Reuters
 Democrats' path to winning the House could rest with progressive candidates challenging Republicans in districts that swung between Trump and Joe Biden.
 In California's 22nd District, incumbent Rep. David Valadao faces Democratic challenger Randy Villegas, who has Sen. Bernie Sanders' endorsement.
 In Colorado's 8th District, Rep. Gabe Evans faces Democrat Manny Rutinel, who had campaigned with New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani.
 In Michigan's 7th District, Rep. Tom Barrett is up against Will Lawrence, a longtime liberal activist and former member of the Democratic Socialists of America.
 Republicans are hoping their rivals' political backgrounds are a mismatch in districts that are by and large evenly divided politically.
 2:59 p.m. EST
 3 NASA astronauts cast ballots from the space station
 Astronaut Anil Menon's sleeping compartment aboard the International Space Station doubled as his voting booth. Menon said in a brief video posted via X on Tuesday that he used his computer to fill out and submit an electronic ballot to Harris County, Texas. Crewmates Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney did the same.
 Harris County is home to NASA's Johnson Space Center and Mission Control.
 U.S. astronauts have been voting in space since 1997.
 Values motivate Texas voters — but for different candidates
 In the Dallas suburbs, two voters say Christian values factored into their votes.
 James Bender said he wants the country to get back to an identity rooted in Judeo-Christian values.
 He said he respected Talarico's religious roots and faith but said, "At the end of the day, I just, I don't agree with him."
 Bender, 47, said he wasn't voting for Paxton's character as much as the policies he'd try to enact if elected.
 Paxton has faced a string of legal and ethical problems and allegations of marital infidelity.
 April Vindiola said those issues made Paxton a "no" for her. She said a candidate's morals and values are important.
 "I've been following Talarico for quite some time," Vindiola said. "I think whenever I've heard him speak … it resonates with me what his beliefs are."
 Republican governor hopeful to voters in liberal California: 'Just try it!'
 The last time California elected a Republican to statewide office, George W. Bush was president, entertainer James Brown was still alive and the second "Pirates of the Caribbean" movie was the biggest film of the year.
 Republican Steve Hilton is trying to defy those odds and end his party's 16-year drought in a state with 4.5 million more registered Democratic voters than Republicans.
 He's tried to win over Californians who rarely vote Republican by repeating the motto "Just try it!"; blaming Democratic leadership for the state's high cost of living; and releasing splashy ads, sometimes using AI to mock his Democratic rival, Xavier Becerra.
 Becerra, meanwhile, has campaigned on a promise to uphold the state's status as a liberal counterweight to Trump's policies. He's tried to tie Hilton to Trump, who endorsed him in the primary.
 California billionaire tax proposal tests voters' appetite to 'tax the rich'
 A cigarette butt is placed on an "I voted" sign during the midterm elections on Skid Row in Los Angeles, California, on Nov. 3, 2026. Photo by Evelyn Hockstein/ Reuters
 The ballot measure, known as Proposition 40, has racked up support from progressives like Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, who has framed it as a monumental step toward reining in deep wealth inequality, while also drawing criticism from Gov. Gavin Newsom and other Democrats, who say it will trigger wealthy people to flee the state.
 The ballot fight has also been defined by the copious amount of money tech moguls and venture capitalists have poured into it. Google co-founder Sergey Brin alone has donated more than $100 million to a political committee working to defeat the proposal.
 The first-in-the-nation measure would levy a one-time, 5% tax on the wealth of Californians whose net worth exceeds $1 billion. Most of the money would be used to backfill federal funding cuts to healthcare, while 10% would go toward education and food assistance programs.
 In Virginia, a retiree says Trump has 'done a great job'
 Joni Borrell, 67, and her father, Herman Jamerson, 91, described themselves as solidly Republican. They voted that way a week before Election Day, casting ballots in Henrico, Virginia, for GOP Rep. Rob Wittman and Bert Mizusawa, the Republican mounting a long-shot bid against Democratic incumbent Sen. Mark Warner.
 Jamerson, a retired plumbing contractor, said he thinks the president has "done a great job" so far this term.
 "He's for the common person. To me, that's his biggest success. I mean, he looks out for the little guy, just the average person," Jamerson said.
 As for Trump and the economy, Jamerson added: "Well, he ain't done yet, that's the thing. And it was in such a mess."
 Borrell, a retired nurse who now works with youth camps, said her strong objections to Democratic Gov. Abigail Spanberger factored into her vote. Keeping Republicans in control of Washington would help preserve some "balance," she said.
 Missouri could undo its amendment protecting the right to abortion
 Abortion is on the ballot in four states including Missouri, where voters are being asked to erase the constitutional right to abortion they adopted two years ago.
 The Republican-dominated state legislature advanced the measure, which also would write into the state constitution a ban on much gender-affirming healthcare for transgender minors.
 Conservative Idaho's question would remove a ban if it were adopted.
 READ MORE: A guide to the key ballot measures voters will decide on Election Day 
 A measure in Nevada would ensure access until at least fetal viability and one in Virginia would create a right to abortion for the first two trimesters of pregnancy.
 Since the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022 and allowed enforcement of state abortion bans, abortion-rights supporters have prevailed on 14 of the 17 ballot measures across the U.S.
 2:23 p.m. EST
 Trump is miffed about reaction to his Reflecting Pool speech
 Trump spent part of Election Day complaining about reaction to his Monday speech at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, criticizing a news outlet and a Democratic congressman.
 Trump spoke in great detail on social media about his upgrades to infrastructure and plumbing at the Reflecting Pool, devoting more time to that project than to Republican candidates he hopes will help the party retain control of Congress.
 WATCH: Trump officially reopens Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool on eve of midterm elections 
 Trump ripped the Daily Mail for describing the speech as a "final midterms speech." He said his rallies Sunday in Iowa and Kansas were meant to close out the campaign.
 He also went after Rep. Ted Lieu, D-Calif., who on social media shared an edited clip of Trump suggesting he might rename the iconic spot on the National Mall the "Trump Reflecting Pool."
 Trump followed up by saying he was joking.
 "I said, very clearly, 'I'm joking,'" he wrote.
 What is The Voter Poll and when will we start to get results?
 Later tonight, we'll start sharing data from The AP Voter Poll, a large survey of verified voters conducted for The Associated Press and the major broadcast news networks.
 It's a high-quality preelection survey of voters merged with the best practices of the historic exit poll, which major broadcasters have relied on for decades. Reflecting the complexity of American elections, it uses a combination of methods to find voters no matter how they cast a ballot, whether early, by mail or on Election Day.
 We'll start sharing data around 5 p.m. EST.
 Oklahoma City man charged with mailing letters with nonhazardous powder to officials before the election
 An Oklahoma City man is charged with sending hundreds of letters containing nonhazardous white powder to public officials ahead of the 2024 and 2026 elections.
 The powders turned out to be yeast or flour, though not all letters have been fully tested, the FBI said in a court filing.
 READ MORE: Man charged with mailing hundreds of letters containing powder to officials ahead of the election 
 Robin Martin is charged with conveying a hoax and mailing threatening communications. He was in custody, and online records didn't list an attorney who could comment on his behalf. He is expected to make an appearance Tuesday in U.S. District Court in Oklahoma City.
 Authorities said last month that they were investigating suspicious letters mailed to congressional and election offices nationwide and urged recipients to treat the mailings as "potentially hazardous."
 Some letters bore ominous messages that could only be read under ultraviolet light. The sender wrote a return address as "U.S.T.E.A., United States Traitor Elimination Army, Takoma Park, MD."
 Texas voters offer two takes on Talarico
 Outside an early voting site in Dripping Springs, Texas, 25-year-old Ian Brown said he had just voted for a straight Republican ticket.
 He referenced some of Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico's past statements about God and gender, which Republican Ken Paxton has highlighted in attack ads.
 "He claims he's Christian, but he says you know there's multiple genders. That's not even biblically accurate," Brown said.
 READ MORE: Paxton and Talarico tussle for Texas Senate seat as Trump campaigns virtually 
 The self-described Republican Libertarian said he thinks Trump is "the best thing for our country right now."
 Sofia Sites, meanwhile, voted for the first time this election and supported Democrats.
 Sites, 21, has a transgender sibling, and Talarico's stance on transgender and LGBTQ+ rights was something that drew her to him, she said.
 "There's no perfect politician; there's no one I like to bow down to," Sites said. "I just think that I'm wanting to see more empathy.
 Voting machine programming blamed for election issues in a New York county
 The vote-counting issues bedeviling Westchester County stem from a program update that happened after polling equipment was initially prepared and tested, according to the state Board of Elections.
 A change in an unnamed local race required an update that wasn't made to machines in other counties, the board said. As a result, those tabulators were unable to recognize completed Election Day ballots.
 State officials said they're working with their counterparts in Westchester County to restore ballot-scanning capability to at least one vote-counting machine at every polling location. Voting continues through established emergency ballot procedures.
 Westchester County Executive Ken Jenkins vowed to launch a bipartisan investigation into what he called a "debacle."
 Arizona voter hopes to see a 'more conservative' government after the election
 John Shaw of Phoenix said he showed up to the polls on Tuesday to support "American values" and "patriotic things."
 Shaw, who declined to say which candidates he picked, said he hoped to see government "be a little more conservative" and to see "less government" overall after the election.
 Democratic Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs is seeking a second term but faces a challenge from Republican Rep. Andy Biggs. Voters will also decide a full slate of contests, including congressional and state legislative races that could shift the balance of power both in Washington and in the state government.
 While there were long lines at Shaw's polling place, he said it was still exciting to talk to fellow voters.
 Democrats make push in Alaska Senate, gubernatorial races
 Alaska voters last elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate in 2008 and as governor in 1998. But Democrats are making strong pushes in both races ahead of the ranked choice general election.
 In the Senate race, two-term Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan has gotten support from Trump and Vance as he seeks to fend off Democrat Mary Peltola, a former congresswoman. Peltola finished first in August's open primary.
 Two other candidates, including another Dan Sullivan, also are running but have done almost no campaigning. Trump has directed the Justice Department to investigate the presence of another candidate with the same name as the incumbent, even calling for Peltola's prosecution. He also continued voicing his opposition to the state's use of ranked voting.
 State Republican leaders have long expressed skepticism about ranked voting but encouraged voters to rank the Republicans. Many Republicans see the strategy as essential to winning the governor's race, featuring Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins and three Republicans, including Trump-backed Bernadette Wilson.
 1:27 p.m. EST
 Georgia Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff seeks a second term against GOP Rep. Mike Collins
 A year ago, Ossoff was considered Democrats' most vulnerable incumbent. The campaign hasn't turned out that way.
 Ossoff had no primary opposition, and he quickly became a fundraising machine, exciting Democrats nationally with his broadsides against Trump. He collected at least $109 million, tops among all Senate candidates.
 Republicans had an extended primary battle. Rep. Mike Collins, a self-declared "MAGA warrior" who echoes Trump's 2020 election denial, received the president's late endorsement and defeated Derek Dooley.
 Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp, the Republican whom GOP leaders wanted to run, backed Dooley and spent the spring telling voters Collins couldn't win in November.
 Collins struggled to hit the $10 million fundraising mark, and he was dogged by questions about an unresolved House ethics investigation and his ties to white nationalists.
 Ossoff is trying to capitalize on Election Day as some Democrats openly hope he runs for president in 2028.
 2 states could ban transgender girls from girls' sports
 Voters in reliably Democratic Colorado and Washington are deciding on ballot measures that would ban transgender girls from girls' sports competitions.
 Both supporters and opponents say that if one or both are adopted, it could open the door to further measures in Democratic-led states in coming elections.
 Similar measures are on the ballot in Arizona, where voters are being asked to apply an existing ban to private schools, and in Nebraska, where a measure would add an existing ban in state law to the state constitution.
 Every state where both the legislature and governor's office are held by Republicans has already passed a law like this. But no state has done it through a ballot question so far.
 The votes come at a time when a growing number of Democratic politicians are saying transgender girls shouldn't be allowed to play girls' sports.
 1:10 p.m. EST
 Vance's Election Day message makes misleading claims about tax cuts
 Vice President JD Vance speak during a campaign rally ahead of the midterm elections at Eugene F. Kranz Toledo Express Airport in Swanton, Ohio, on Nov. 2, 2026. Photo by Tom Brenner/ Pool via Reuters
 In a post on X, the vice president sought to remind voters about the Trump administration's effort to cut taxes over the past year and a half.
 "We ended taxes on overtime. We ended taxes on tips. We ended taxes on Social Security," Vance wrote on the social media platform.
 But the changes made by the wide-ranging tax law enacted by Trump are not that clear-cut.
 More than 40 states have not implemented the federal law ending taxes on tips, meaning workers who receive a federal tax deduction for tips or overtime still will owe state taxes on those earnings.
 As for taxes on Social Security, the legislation targeted seniors' income with a temporary benefit, not just Social Security.
 12:57 p.m. EST
 Data center backlash may be a potent election issue
 Opposition to data centers in communities across the U.S. has snowballed from a local issue into a midterm election weapon in statewide races from Texas to Ohio to Florida amid the artificial intelligence revolution.
 Candidates spent millions to paint their opponents as data center patsies — giving them nicknames like "Data Nate" — as onetime data center boosters worked to distance themselves or get tough on the industry.
 READ MORE: Trump keeps embracing data centers, an unpopular topic in midterm races 
 They had an ally: Trump urged communities to accept data centers, as the industry spent millions to boost its image.
 Meanwhile, the issue crossed traditional ideological boundaries.
 Labor unions became allies of tech giants, as they scrambled to build the behemoth projects.
 Clean energy advocates became staunch critics of data centers, as energy-hungry server warehouses set off the biggest-ever construction boom of natural gas-fired power plants. Ranchers and farmers worried about water shortages or losing agricultural land.
 Pennsylvania man says he voted to stop Trump
 Kim Dean, 74, is a Democrat who voted for Kamala Harris in 2024 but says he's never voted strictly for Democrats — until this year.
 Dean has a long list of grievances about how Trump has governed: the way U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement is "running around" and deporting people, the president "tearing down" the White House, the war in Iran, the way Trump "berates" people.
 "A lot of this stuff, I just don't agree with it. It just don't make sense to me," the retired steel worker from Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, said after dropping off his mail ballot.
 "I'll be honest with you, I would have voted for Pepe the dog this year, you know what I mean? To try to get this administration changed. Yes, I'm voting against the whole administration."
 Aided by Trump's super PAC, Republicans outraised Democrats
 If Republicans lose ground in Congress, it won't be because they didn't have more money than Democrats.
 Republicans have held a financial advantage leading up to the midterm elections, owing to GOP-aligned outside groups' outsized role, notably in Senate races.
 Combined, the Republican National Committee, its related congressional committees and corresponding super PACs, including Trump's MAGA Inc., raised more than $2.2 billion, compared with about $1.3 billion for the Democratic National Committee and its aligned committees and groups.
 READ MORE: Trump's political groups spend nearly $277 million in late midterm blitz on behalf of GOP candidates 
 Democratic candidates, however, have outraised Republicans in their individual races, more than $2.3 billion to about $1.6 billion. That money goes further than super PAC dollars because candidates get lower advertising rates.
 The two sides have spent an astronomical amount on the midterm campaigns — more than $11.9 billion, according to Federal Election Commission records. The vast majority of spending has been on advertising: Republicans and allied groups have spent more than $5.5 billion while Democrats and allied groups have spent a little more than $5 billion, according to the media-tracking firm AdImpact.
 Man charged with mailing hundreds of letters containing powder to officials ahead of the election
 Federal authorities have charged an Oklahoma man with sending hundreds of letters containing nonhazardous white powder to public officials ahead of the 2024 and 2026 elections.
 The powders turned out to be yeast or flour, though not all letters have been fully tested, the FBI said in a court filing made public Tuesday.
 Robin Martin is charged with conveying a hoax and mailing threatening communications. Martin was expected to make his initial court appearance Tuesday afternoon in Oklahoma City. Online records do not list an attorney to comment on his behalf.
 Democrats aim to capture a majority of governors' offices for first time since 2006
 If they pull it off, it would be the first time in two decades that Democrats hold a majority of the governors' offices.
 All told, 36 states will elect a governor on Nov. 3. Heading into the elections, Republicans held a 26-24 majority. Democrats need to pick up two more states to capture a majority. Democrats last gained a majority in 2006 and lost it four years later.
 The parties see about a dozen races as competitive.
 Democrats' best opportunities to pick up a governor's office are in Alaska, Georgia, Iowa, Nevada and Ohio.
 Republicans' best opportunity to capture an executive suite is in Kansas.
 A man walks outside a polling station during the midterm elections on Election Day in Overland Park, Kansas, on Nov. 3, 2026. Photo by Nathan Howard/ Reuters
 Next on the GOP's list are Wisconsin's and Michigan's open governor's offices.
 Democrats think they have a chance in Texas, Florida, Oklahoma and Nebraska.
 12:06 p.m. EST
 Helicopter to help South Carolina island count votes faster
 Several hundred ballots from South Carolina's most remote precinct should be counted a lot faster Tuesday night thanks to the local sheriff's office helicopter.

 There are no bridges to Daufuskie Island on the far southern coast of the state. In previous elections, voting officials had to collect ballots and other equipment and wait for the regular ferry schedule or another boat, which could delay results for five hours.

 A look at recent midterm election results
 Midterm elections generally favor the party that doesn't hold the White House, but the two most recent cycles generated a mixed result.
 When Joe Biden was president, Republicans won control of the House in 2022, picking up nine seats and assuming a slim majority. But Democrats maintained control of the Senate and even picked up a seat in the chamber.
 A similar dynamic occurred during Trump's first term, though the gains were much larger for Democrats in the House. They netted 40 seats in the 2018 midterms and took the majority for the first time in eight years. Still, Republicans expanded their Senate majority by two seats.
 Some analysts see similarities between this midterm political environment and that of 2006, when President George W. Bush and Republicans faced headwinds from high fuel prices and the war in Iraq. That year, Democrats added 30 House seats and six Senate seats to take the majority in both chambers.
